1.q: An operative is told to flush little-used outlets 'when they get a chance'. Why is a fixed schedule better?
o: It makes sure every outlet is flushed at least weekly and none is forgotten
It reduces the number of outlets needing flushing
It looks more professional on paper only
It lets outlets be skipped when busy
1.w: A fixed schedule ensures every little-used outlet is flushed at least weekly and none is overlooked.

n.2: The benefit is real control, not just paperwork appearance.
n.3: A good schedule prevents skipping, it does not permit it.
n.1: A schedule does not change how many outlets exist.

1.q: Two operatives disagree on how long to hold the disinfectant during a chlorination. One says 'until it looks done', the other wants to follow the stated contact time. Who is right and why?
o: The first, because visual judgement is faster
Whoever is more senior, regardless of the method
Neither, as contact time does not affect disinfection
The second, because the stated contact time is what makes the process effective
1.w: The disinfectant must be held for the stated contact time; effectiveness depends on concentration maintained over that defined time, not on how the water looks.

n.0: Water does not visibly show when disinfection is complete; the stated contact time governs it.
n.2: Contact time is central to disinfection; without it the process is unreliable.
n.1: Seniority does not override the written method's stated contact time.

1.q: A sink has been removed but the pipe that fed it has been capped just below the old tap position. What should be done?
o: Insulate the capped pipe and take no further action
Leave the capped pipe as it is
Cut the redundant pipe back to the live main and cap it there
Open the cap once a month to let air in
1.w: The disused branch should be removed back to the live main so no stagnant dead leg is left.

n.1: Leaving the long capped stub leaves stagnant water that can grow legionella.
n.3: Letting air in does not refresh the water and does not fix the dead leg.
n.0: Insulation alone does not remove the stagnant water inside the redundant pipe.

1.q: The written scheme for controlling Legionella risk must set out several things. Which of the following is one of them?
o: The postcode lottery results for the local area
The marketing plan for the building's owner
The purchase price of every fitting in the building
The clear allocation of responsibilities for carrying out the control measures
1.w: The written scheme must set out the control measures, how and when they are checked and monitored, and who is responsible for carrying them out — clear allocation of duties is a required element.

n.2: The cost of fittings is not a control-scheme requirement.
n.1: A marketing plan has nothing to do with managing water risk.
n.0: This is irrelevant filler with no bearing on the scheme.

1.q: Which of these is a common source of legionella-carrying aerosols?
o: A dry electrical socket
Showers
A closed metal filing cabinet
A sealed bottle of unopened water
1.w: Showers create a fine spray that can carry legionella into the air where it may be inhaled.

n.3: A sealed, unopened bottle produces no aerosol.
n.0: A dry socket has no water and makes no spray.
n.2: A filing cabinet is not a water source.

1.q: Overall, what do complete and honest monitoring records give the responsible person?
o: Confidence that controls are working and evidence to prove compliance
Permission to ignore action levels
A reason to stop inspecting the system
A way to avoid training staff
1.w: Accurate records show the controls are effective and provide the documented proof of compliance the responsible person needs.

n.2: Good records support continued inspection, not stopping it.
n.3: Records do not remove the need to train competent staff.
n.1: Action levels must always be acted on, whatever the records show.

1.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, an employer's duty to non-employees such as visitors and the public is:
o: To conduct the undertaking so they are not exposed to risks to their health and safety, so far as is reasonably practicable
Non-existent, as the Act only protects employees
Only owed to paying customers
Limited to putting up a warning sign
1.w: Section 3 extends the duty to persons not in the employer's employment who may be affected by the work.

n.1: The Act clearly protects people beyond the direct employees.
n.3: A sign alone does not discharge the wider duty to control the risk.
n.2: The duty is owed to anyone affected, not only paying customers.

1.q: At a large site, taps at the far end of a wing run only warm even after running for a while, while taps near the plant room run hot quickly. This most likely points to:
o: The calorifier being stored far too hot
The cold water supply being switched off
A problem with the secondary circulation reaching that wing
Too much sludge in the tap spouts
1.w: Distant outlets that never get properly hot suggest the secondary circulation is not maintaining temperature to that part of the building.

n.0: If storage were too hot, distant taps would tend to run hotter, not cooler.
n.3: Warm-not-hot water across a whole wing points to circulation, not sludge in individual spouts.
n.1: A cold supply being off would affect cold water, not the warmth of the hot outlets.

1.q: A little-used shower is flushed weekly, but its monthly hot check reads 46°C at one minute. What does this reading most likely indicate?
o: The shower should be reclassified as a cold outlet
Hot water is not reaching the required temperature and the result must be reported
The reading proves the weekly flushing regime can now be stopped
The outlet is fully compliant because it exceeds 45°C
1.w: A hot outlet must reach 50°C within one minute; 46°C falls short and sits within the danger zone, so the shortfall must be recorded and reported for investigation.

n.3: Exceeding 45°C is not the standard; hot delivery must reach 50°C, so 46°C fails.
n.2: A failing temperature is a reason to maintain controls, not to stop flushing a little-used outlet.
n.0: A hot outlet that underperforms is not reclassified as cold; the hot fault is investigated.

1.q: Under the ACOP L8 approach, which should you try to do FIRST when managing legionella risk?
o: Wait until a case of illness is reported
Prevent the risk where reasonably practicable, then control what remains
Add extra biocide to every part of the system
Fit more monitoring meters before doing anything else
1.w: You should prevent the risk of exposure so far as is reasonably practicable first, and control any risk that cannot be prevented.

n.3: Monitoring measures a risk but does not prevent or control it on its own.
n.2: Dosing biocide everywhere is a control, not the first-choice prevention step.
n.0: Waiting for illness means the risk was never managed.

1.q: A basin TMV is delivering water at 47°C to a dementia care unit. How should this reading be treated?
o: Ignore it, because basin temperatures are not part of scald control
Acceptable, as anything under 50°C is regarded as safe for bathing
Acceptable, provided the hot feed to the valve is below 60°C
Too hot for the at-risk users – investigate and recommission the valve to the safe range
1.w: 47°C is above the safe blended range and presents a scald risk to vulnerable users, so the valve needs investigating and recommissioning back to the correct delivery temperature.

n.1: Under 50°C is not automatically safe; safe basin delivery is around 41°C, and 47°C can scald at-risk users.
n.2: The hot feed should be hot (near 60°C); a below-60°C feed would not make a 47°C delivery acceptable and would signal other problems.
n.0: Basin delivery temperature to vulnerable users is exactly what TMV scald control addresses.

1.q: A designer wants to reduce stagnation risk in a new washroom. Which design principle aligns with HSG274 Part 2?
o: Minimise pipe run lengths and stored volume so water is turned over quickly
Route long individual branches to each outlet for future flexibility
Provide generous spare capacity by oversizing pipes for possible future demand
Add several capped spur connections for future appliances
1.w: Good design minimises pipe length, dead legs and stored volume so that water is used and replaced frequently, keeping it moving and reducing the chance of it reaching growth temperatures.

n.2: Oversizing lowers turnover and promotes stagnation and warming.
n.1: Long individual branches create low-turnover legs that stagnate.
n.3: Capped spurs are dead legs in waiting and should be avoided, not designed in.

1.q: Cold water should be stored and distributed below which temperature to limit bacterial growth?
1.w: Keeping cold water below 20°C limits the growth of Legionella and other bacteria, which multiply fastest between roughly 20°C and 45°C.

n.0: 30°C is well inside the range where bacteria multiply readily.
n.2: 45°C is near the top of the growth range and far too warm for stored cold water.
n.3: 5°C is colder than required; the recognised control limit for cold water is below 20°C, not 5°C.

1.q: What is the main reason records of calorifier temperatures and cleaning should be kept as part of the water safety scheme?
o: Only to satisfy the water supplier's billing
To demonstrate the control scheme is being followed and to reveal trends before they become failures
To decide when to replace the outlet taps
To calculate the building's energy bills
1.w: Records provide evidence that monitoring and cleaning are being carried out as required, and reviewing them reveals adverse trends, such as a slowly falling return temperature, so action can be taken before a control failure occurs.

n.3: Records support legionella control and compliance, not energy bill calculation.
n.0: They exist for the water safety scheme and legal duty of care, not for the water supplier's billing.
n.2: Tap replacement is a maintenance decision, not the purpose of temperature and cleaning records.

1.q: You open last month's monitoring sheet and find it completely blank with no readings. What is the correct action?
o: Report the gap to the responsible person so the missed monitoring can be addressed
Throw the sheet away and start fresh
Fill it in now with made-up figures for last month
Copy this month's readings into last month's boxes
1.w: A missed set of records is a real gap in evidence and must be reported so it can be investigated and put right, never fabricated.

n.2: Inventing past figures is falsification and misleads everyone relying on the record.
n.1: Destroying the sheet removes evidence that monitoring was missed.
n.3: Copying current readings into a past month falsifies the history.

1.q: Why does scale build-up inside a system raise Legionella risk?
o: It keeps the water permanently above 60°C
Its rough surface shelters bacteria and provides nutrients for growth
It removes all nutrients from the water
It stops water flowing anywhere in the building
1.w: Scale gives the bacteria a rough, sheltered, nutrient-rich surface to colonise.

n.0: Scale does not heat water, it insulates and harbours deposits.
n.2: Scale adds surface and nutrients, it does not strip them out.
n.3: Scale restricts flow locally but does not stop all flow in a building.

1.q: Which combination of personal factors is most strongly associated with a higher risk of serious Legionella illness?
o: Being over 45, a smoker and having a weakened immune system
Being physically active with no chronic conditions
Being teetotal with no history of lung or heart disease
Being under 25, female and a non-smoker
1.w: Being over 45, smoking and having a weakened immune system are all recognised factors that combine to raise the risk of serious illness from Legionella.

n.3: Younger, female non-smokers are generally at lower risk of severe illness.
n.1: Being active with no chronic conditions is associated with lower risk.
n.2: Avoiding alcohol and having no lung or heart disease are protective rather than risk-raising.

1.q: An overflow (warning) pipe should be arranged so that:
o: It runs uphill from the tank to the roof
It is screened and turns down to discharge visibly to warn of a fault
It discharges directly into the nearest foul drain
It is left open and unscreened for maximum airflow
1.w: A warning pipe is screened against insects and turns down to a visible discharge point so an overflow is noticed and does not become an entry route.

n.2: Connecting straight into a drain risks back-siphonage of contaminated water and hides the warning.
n.0: An overflow must fall away from the tank; it cannot run uphill and drain.
n.3: Leaving it open and unscreened invites insects and vermin into the tank.

1.q: At roughly what temperature is legionella killed quickly?
o: 60°C and above
1.w: Water at 60°C and above kills legionella quickly, which is why hot water should be stored hot.

n.3: 37°C is close to the ideal temperature for growth, not for killing the bacteria.
n.0: At 20°C the bacteria begin to multiply rather than die.
n.1: At 10°C the bacteria are dormant but not killed.

1.q: A care home manager asks an operative to turn the hot water cylinder down to 45°C so frail residents cannot be scalded. What is the correct response?
o: Switch the hot water off during the day
Turn the cylinder down to 50°C as a compromise
Turn the cylinder down to 45°C as requested
Keep storage at 60°C or above and fit TMVs to the residents' outlets
1.w: Storage must stay at 60°C or above for legionella control, and scalding is prevented with TMVs at the outlets.

n.2: Storing at 45°C sits in the legionella growth range and is unsafe.
n.1: 50°C storage is still below the 60°C needed to control legionella.
n.0: Switching hot water off does not control legionella and disrupts the water supply.

1.q: A room's shower will be permanently taken out of service in a refurbishment. What is the correct hygiene outcome?
o: Cap the shower off at the wall and leave the pipe behind it
Leave the shower fitted but never flush it
Fill the shower head with sealant
Remove the redundant pipework back to the live main so no dead leg is left
1.w: Redundant pipework should be removed back to the live main so no dead leg of stagnant water is left behind.

n.0: Capping at the wall leaves a dead leg of stagnant water in the pipe.
n.1: Leaving it unflushed creates exactly the stagnant risk to avoid.
n.2: Sealing the head does nothing about the stagnant pipe behind it.

1.q: A legionella sample from a shower has come back positive. What is the appropriate response?
o: Report the result to the responsible person and follow the scheme's actions, which may include disinfection
Remove the shower and throw the sample away
Increase the water pressure to the shower
Do nothing, as one positive result is normal
1.w: A positive result must be escalated to the responsible person and acted on under the scheme, which can include cleaning and disinfection.

n.3: A positive legionella result is a control failure signal and always needs a response.
n.1: Discarding the evidence prevents proper follow-up and investigation.
n.2: Raising the pressure does nothing to remove or kill the legionella present.

1.q: Under COSHH, how often should the assessment for a legionella risk be reviewed?
o: Only once when the building is first built
Only if an outbreak has already occurred
Regularly, and whenever there is reason to think it is no longer valid
Never, once it is signed
1.w: COSHH requires the assessment to be reviewed regularly and whenever it may no longer be valid, such as after changes to the system.

n.0: A single assessment at construction cannot reflect later changes in use or plant.
n.3: Assessments are living documents that must be kept up to date.
n.1: Waiting for an outbreak defeats the purpose of preventive assessment.

1.q: Which statement about preventing legionella risk is correct?
o: Longer runs of unused pipework are always safer
Prevention is impossible, so only monitoring matters
Adding more storage tanks always reduces risk
Removing unnecessary storage and dead-legs helps prevent risk before controls are even needed
1.w: Designing out storage, stagnation and dead-legs prevents conditions for growth, which is preferable to controlling them later.

n.1: Prevention is a recognised and preferred step, not impossible.
n.2: Extra unnecessary storage adds stagnation risk rather than removing it.
n.0: Unused dead-legs stagnate and increase risk, not reduce it.

1.q: Cold water should be kept below which temperature to control Legionella?
o: Below 18°C
Below 25°C
Below 20°C
Below 15°C
1.w: Cold water should be kept below 20°C to stay out of the bacterial growth range.

n.3: Below 15°C is ideal but the control limit is 20°C.
n.0: 18°C is not the recognised limit.
n.1: 25°C is inside the danger zone and unsafe.

2.q: During a monthly check a hot sentinel outlet reaches 50°C only after running for three minutes. How should this be treated?
o: As a cold-water fault to be investigated on the cold side
As a pass, because the outlet eventually reached the 50°C figure
As irrelevant, because only the final steady temperature matters
As a failure of the one-minute criterion that should be recorded and reported
2.w: Hot water must reach 50°C within one minute; taking three minutes fails the time criterion and suggests problems such as a long dead-leg or poor circulation, so it must be recorded and reported.

n.1: Reaching temperature eventually is not a pass; the standard requires 50°C within one minute.
n.2: The time taken to reach temperature is part of the criterion, so it cannot be ignored.
n.0: This is a hot-supply timing issue, not a cold-water fault.

2.q: After building work that generated dust and debris near an open water tank, what is the sensible hygiene step?
o: Leave the tank open to let dust settle out
Assume the lid kept everything out and do nothing
Increase the water temperature in the cold tank
Check the tank for contamination and clean and disinfect it if debris has entered
2.w: Work that could contaminate a system means checking the tank and cleaning and disinfecting it if debris has got in.

n.1: Assuming no ingress without checking risks leaving contamination in place.
n.2: Warming cold stored water moves it into the growth range, worsening risk.
n.0: Leaving the tank open invites more contamination rather than resolving it.

2.q: A maintenance operative removes a redundant length of pipe but leaves a short tee stub about 400 mm long projecting from the live pipe. Why is this still a problem?
o: The stub raises the mains pressure and can burst the fitting
The stub is a residual dead leg holding stagnant water that can warm and colonise
The stub increases flow velocity and erodes the tee joint
The stub reduces the volume of stored water and starves outlets
2.w: Any length of pipe left projecting from the live main forms a residual dead leg that retains stagnant water, warms towards growth temperatures and can seed the live water with legionella. Removal should be flush to the live pipe.

n.2: A short dead stub carries little or no flow; velocity and erosion are not the issue.
n.0: The stub does not raise mains pressure.
n.3: The concern is stagnation in the stub, not any reduction in stored volume.

2.q: Why is it useful to tell a doctor about recent exposure to water aerosols when you feel unwell?
o: It lets them ignore your symptoms
It guarantees you do not have the disease
It replaces the need for any tests
It helps them consider and diagnose Legionnaires' disease quickly
2.w: Mentioning possible aerosol exposure prompts the doctor to consider Legionnaires' disease and arrange the right tests and treatment.

n.0: It should make them take your symptoms more seriously, not less.
n.2: Tests may still be needed to confirm the diagnosis.
n.1: It does not rule the disease out; it helps them check for it.

2.q: During a TMV service, why is the inlet strainer cleaned?
o: A blocked strainer heats the water
A clean strainer changes the water colour
The strainer stores disinfectant
A blocked strainer can restrict flow and affect the blended temperature
2.w: Debris in the strainer disturbs the flow balance and can stop the valve holding a safe blended temperature, so it is cleaned.

n.1: A strainer does not affect water colour.
n.2: A strainer does not store disinfectant.
n.0: A blocked strainer does not heat water; it restricts flow.

2.q: Why is simply raising the temperature briefly sometimes not enough to control Legionella hidden in biofilm?
o: Biofilm makes the bacteria grow faster when heated
Heat cannot affect any bacteria
Biofilm is always above 60°C anyway
The biofilm shelters the bacteria so treatment may not reach them all
2.w: Bacteria protected inside biofilm may not be fully reached by a brief treatment.

n.0: Heat does not make sheltered bacteria multiply.
n.2: Biofilm is not inherently hot, it insulates and shelters.
n.1: Heat does kill exposed bacteria, the issue is reaching the sheltered ones.

2.q: Who should carry out or oversee a legionella risk assessment?
o: A person who is competent, with the right knowledge, skills and experience
Anyone who happens to be free that day
A visitor with no water knowledge
The newest apprentice on their first morning, unsupervised
2.w: The assessment must be done by someone competent, with sufficient knowledge, skills and experience to identify and assess the risk.

n.1: Availability does not make a person competent to assess the risk.
n.2: A visitor without knowledge cannot judge the system's risks.
n.3: An unsupervised first-day apprentice lacks the needed competence.

2.q: Why are flexible flexible-hose connectors (such as those under taps or to appliances) flagged as a specific risk in HSG274 Part 2?
o: The EPDM/rubber lining can degrade and provide nutrients and surfaces that harbour biofilm and legionella
They contain chlorine reservoirs that over-dose the outlet
They cannot be connected to WRAS-approved fittings at all
They are always undersized and therefore raise water velocity too high
2.w: Flexible hoses often use EPDM or similar elastomers that can degrade, shed nutrients and support biofilm and legionella growth; their use should be minimised and approved low-risk types selected.

n.3: The concern is the lining material and biofilm, not excessive velocity.
n.1: They do not store or over-dose chlorine.
n.2: They can be connected to approved fittings; the issue is the hose lining material itself.

2.q: During a monthly check an operative finds the calorifier base drain has never been opened and heavy sediment is suspected. What is the appropriate response?
o: Record it and take no further action
Raise the storage temperature to 90°C instead
Arrange for the base to be drained and de-sludged as part of maintenance
Weld the drain valve shut to stop leaks
2.w: A base that has never been drained should be de-sludged as part of maintenance so bacteria have nowhere to shelter.

n.3: Sealing the drain shut prevents the base ever being cleared of sludge.
n.1: Overheating the store does not remove the settled sludge, which still shelters bacteria.
n.0: Recording without acting leaves the sludge in place and the risk uncontrolled.

2.q: Which document would an operative primarily follow for the day-to-day tasks and frequencies on a site?
o: The company's holiday policy
The site-specific written scheme of control
A generic advertising brochure
The building's fire certificate
2.w: The written scheme of control sets out the specific tasks, methods and frequencies for that site.

n.2: A brochure is marketing material, not a control document.
n.3: A fire certificate concerns fire safety, not legionella control tasks.
n.0: A holiday policy is unrelated to water hygiene tasks.

2.q: Why should records of flushing and cleaning be kept accurate and up to date?
o: So the water bill can be checked
Because the water company demands them each week
To prove the control scheme is being carried out and to spot missed tasks
To show the outlet colour has not changed
2.w: Accurate records prove the control scheme is being followed and help spot any outlets that have been missed.

n.3: Records are not about the colour of the outlet.
n.0: They are not for checking the water bill.
n.1: The reason is legionella control, not a weekly demand from the water company.

2.q: Why can a shower head that has not been used for a long period be a particular Legionella concern when first used again?
o: Because a dry shower head is the ideal place for bacteria to breed
Because stagnation can let bacteria multiply, then the first use releases aerosols
Because unused water becomes too acidic for the bacteria to survive
Because cold, moving mains water is the highest-risk condition
2.w: Stagnant water in a little-used outlet can allow Legionella to multiply, and the first use then discharges an aerosol that may carry the bacteria into the air to be inhaled.

n.2: Stagnation does not reliably make water too acidic; it tends to favour growth.
n.0: Legionella needs water to multiply, not a dry head.
n.3: Cold, flowing mains water is comparatively low risk; stagnant warm water is the concern.

2.q: On a calorifier (hot water storage vessel), which temperatures are typically monitored as part of temperature control?
o: The flow and return temperatures
The brand name printed on the label
The colour of the outer casing
The weight of the vessel when full
2.w: Calorifier flow and return temperatures are checked to confirm the stored hot water is being kept hot enough.

n.2: The casing colour tells you nothing about water temperature.
n.3: The vessel's weight is not a temperature control measure.
n.1: The brand name has no bearing on temperature control.

2.q: Under Section 7 of the HSWA 1974, what duties are placed directly on employees such as water hygiene operatives?
o: No duties at all, as all duties rest solely with the employer
To personally fund any safety equipment they need
To take reasonable care of their own and others' safety and to cooperate with their employer on health and safety
To design the entire Legionella control scheme themselves
2.w: Section 7 places duties on employees to take reasonable care for the health and safety of themselves and others affected by their acts, and to cooperate with the employer on health and safety matters.

n.3: Designing the whole control scheme is a duty-holder/management function, not the individual employee's Section 7 duty.
n.0: Employees do have personal legal duties under the Act.
n.1: Employers, not employees, are responsible for providing necessary safety equipment.

2.q: A school is closed over a long summer holiday. What should the written scheme cover for this period?
o: Keeping water moving, for example flushing outlets, so it does not stagnate while the building is empty
Removing the risk assessment for the holiday
Leaving every tap running continuously day and night
Switching off all record keeping until term starts
2.w: During long closures the scheme should keep water fresh, such as by regular flushing, to prevent stagnation.

n.3: Records should continue, as the risk does not stop over the holiday.
n.1: Removing the assessment leaves the closure unmanaged.
n.2: Leaving all taps running wastes water and is not the specified control.

2.q: What is a typical safe delivery temperature for a TMV-served bath or shower used by vulnerable people?
o: Around 55°C
Around 20°C
Around 41°C
Around 60°C
2.w: Blended delivery of roughly 41°C gives a warm, usable temperature that is well below the scalding threshold.

n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature and would scald.
n.1: 20°C is cold water territory, not a usable bath or shower temperature.
n.0: 55°C is close to the distribution temperature and would present a scald risk.

2.q: You find a wasps' nest built inside a tank vent where no screen is fitted. What does this tell you?
o: The overflow pipe is working correctly
The tank is the correct size for the demand
The tank water is too cold for bacteria
The vent needs a screen fitted to stop insects entering the tank
2.w: Insects nesting in the vent show the opening is unprotected, so a screen must be fitted to keep insects out of the stored water.

n.2: An insect nest tells you nothing about water temperature.
n.0: An unscreened, nested vent is a fault, not evidence the overflow works.
n.1: Insect ingress is unrelated to whether the tank is correctly sized.

2.q: Thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) appear on the maintenance schedule. Which of the following should be checked and recorded as part of their routine servicing?
o: That the blended outlet temperature is within the safe range and the fail-safe still shuts off
That the valve reduces the incoming mains pressure to a fixed value
That the valve carries the installer's business card in a nearby cupboard
That the valve body is painted the correct colour for the room
2.w: TMV servicing checks the blended temperature is correct for the application and that the thermal shut-off operates, because a failed TMV can deliver water at a temperature favouring legionella or cause scalding.

n.3: The colour of the valve body has no bearing on temperature control or safety.
n.2: A nearby business card is not a functional or recordable safety check.
n.1: A TMV blends hot and cold to a safe temperature; pressure reduction is a separate device's function.

2.q: Which action helps maintain good turnover and reduce stagnation in a storage tank?
o: Keeping the tank permanently brim full and unused
Fitting the largest tank that will physically fit
Sizing the tank to match real daily demand
Blocking off the outlet to save water
2.w: Matching tank size to genuine daily demand keeps the stored water moving and refreshed, reducing the time it sits and warms.

n.1: An over-large tank stores water that is not used and encourages stagnation.
n.0: A full, unused tank is the definition of stagnant storage.
n.3: Blocking the outlet stops turnover entirely and would let the water stagnate.

2.q: An operative is offered a shortcut that skips part of the written disinfection procedure to finish before lunch. What should they do?
o: Skip the flushing step only
Take the shortcut, as the result is probably fine
Halve every contact time to save time
Follow the full written procedure; skipping steps can leave the system unsafe
2.w: The full written procedure must be followed, because omitting steps can leave the system inadequately disinfected and unsafe.

n.1: A shortcut that skips steps risks an ineffective disinfection despite appearances.
n.0: Skipping flushing can leave harmful chemical in the supply.
n.2: Halving contact times may mean the disinfectant has not acted long enough to work.

2.q: Pontiac fever is best described as which of the following?
o: An allergic reaction to chlorine used in water treatment
A skin infection caught by touching contaminated water
A more severe, rapidly fatal form of Legionella infection
A milder, self-limiting illness caused by Legionella without the pneumonia
2.w: Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limiting flu-like illness caused by Legionella that does not develop into the pneumonia seen in Legionnaires' disease.

n.2: Pontiac fever is milder, not more severe, and is not typically fatal.
n.0: It is caused by Legionella, not by an allergic reaction to chlorine.
n.1: It results from inhaling aerosols, not skin contact, and is not a skin infection.

2.q: What is the purpose of a flow straightener or aerator fitted into the nose of a tap, and why must it be kept clean?
o: It measures flow rate for billing and must be left sealed
It sterilises the water chemically, so cleaning would remove its protection
It smooths and shapes the flow but traps debris and scale, so it must be cleaned and disinfected on the same schedule as the outlet
It heats the water at the outlet, so it should never be disturbed
2.w: Aerators and flow straighteners shape the stream but present a large fine-mesh surface that collects scale, grit and biofilm; they must be cleaned, descaled and disinfected on the same routine as the rest of the outlet.

n.1: These are mechanical fittings; they do not chemically sterilise the water.
n.3: They do not heat the water and are designed to be removed for cleaning.
n.0: They are not metering devices; leaving them sealed and dirty creates a fouling reservoir at the outlet.

2.q: A monthly sentinel temperature is defined as being taken at which outlets?
o: The outlets nearest to and furthest from each hot and cold supply
The outlet with the newest tap
Only the outlet in the manager's office
Every single outlet in the building each month
2.w: Sentinel outlets are the nearest and furthest points on each supply, which represent the extremes of the system's performance.

n.2: A single chosen office does not represent the system extremes.
n.3: Checking every outlet monthly is not what sentinel monitoring means.
n.1: The age of the tap does not define a sentinel point.

2.q: Why is around 37°C an especially dangerous water temperature?
o: It matches human body temperature and is where Legionella multiplies fastest
It is the legal minimum for hot water storage
It is too cold for any bacteria to survive
It is the temperature at which Legionella is instantly killed
2.w: Around 37°C is close to body temperature and is the ideal condition for the fastest Legionella growth.

n.3: Legionella is not killed at 37°C, it thrives there.
n.2: 37°C is warm, well within the range bacteria multiply in.
n.1: The storage requirement for hot water is 60°C, not 37°C.

2.q: Which statement about a hot water calorifier is correct?
o: It should be run cold to prevent any risk of scalding
It should keep the water lukewarm to save on fuel
It should heat the stored water so it is delivered hot to the system
It is only used to store cold drinking water
2.w: A calorifier's job is to heat and store water so it reaches the outlets hot enough to control bacteria.

n.1: Lukewarm water sits in the growth range and is unsafe.
n.3: A calorifier stores hot water, not cold drinking water.
n.0: Running it cold would encourage bacteria; scalding is controlled by mixing valves, not by cooling storage.

3.q: Why are older adults more likely to become seriously ill from legionella than young adults?
o: They breathe more contaminated water on purpose
Age has no effect at all
Their body defences are often weaker, so infection can take hold more easily
They always work near cooling towers
3.w: As people age their natural defences tend to weaken, making serious Legionnaires' disease more likely.

n.0: They do not deliberately inhale more contaminated water; their susceptibility is higher.
n.1: Age is a recognised risk factor, so it clearly has an effect.
n.3: Their workplace is not the reason; reduced resistance is.

3.q: How long should water hygiene monitoring records generally be kept?
o: For a suitable retention period, typically at least five years
Only until the end of the working day
They do not need to be kept at all
No longer than one week
3.w: Records should be retained for a suitable period, commonly at least five years, so trends and compliance can be reviewed.

n.1: A single day gives no history to review.
n.3: A week is far too short to show trends or prove ongoing compliance.
n.2: Records must be kept; they are the evidence of control.

3.q: While inspecting a cold water storage tank you find it visibly dirty, with debris and biofilm. What does finding a tank in this condition require?
o: Leaving it until the next scheduled annual inspection
Adding a little more disinfectant to the incoming supply
Simply topping the tank up with fresh water
Cleaning and disinfection of the tank
3.w: Finding a tank or system dirty is a trigger for cleaning and disinfection; the tank is cleaned out and disinfected rather than left in a fouled state.

n.2: Topping up does not remove the debris and biofilm already present.
n.0: A known dirty tank should not be left uncontrolled until a future date.
n.1: Dosing the supply does not clean an already-fouled tank; it must be cleaned and disinfected.

3.q: Why does the whole volume of water in a calorifier need to reach the control temperature, not just the top?
o: Because the flow pipe draws from the coldest layer
Because cooler layers, especially at the base, can let legionella survive
Because only the base water reaches the taps
Because the top layer cools down fastest
3.w: If cooler layers remain, particularly at the base, legionella can survive there, so the whole volume must reach temperature.

n.3: The concern is the cool base surviving, not the top cooling fastest.
n.2: Water is drawn from the hotter upper region, but any surviving bacteria at the base can still spread through the system.
n.0: The flow normally draws from the hotter top, which is why the neglected base is the risk.

3.q: In a dead leg with no through-flow, how does any fresh water reach the closed end?
o: Only very slowly by diffusion, so the water effectively stagnates
Quickly, because pressure pushes it through the closed end
It is pumped through on a timed cycle automatically
It cannot warm up because no water reaches it at all
3.w: With no outlet drawing water through, the closed end is refreshed only by slow diffusion, so it stagnates.

n.1: A closed end has no exit, so pressure cannot push a flow through it.
n.2: There is no automatic timed cycle on an ordinary dead leg.
n.3: Water does reach it and sits there warming to the surrounding temperature.

3.q: During a routine tank inspection, which of these should be checked?
o: Lid fit, screens, water clarity, temperature and material condition
Nothing internal, to avoid disturbing the water
Only the colour of the outside of the tank
Just the name of the plumber who fitted it
3.w: A proper inspection covers the lid fit, insect screens, clarity of the water, temperature and the condition of the tank and its fittings.

n.2: External colour alone tells you nothing about the hygiene of the stored water.
n.3: Who fitted the tank is not a condition check.
n.1: The inside condition, clarity and temperature must be checked, carefully, not avoided.

3.q: A supervisor tells you to skip a scheduled temperature monitoring round because 'it's always fine'. What should you do?
o: Do half of the outlets to save time
Skip it as instructed and record it as done
Delete the outlet from the record permanently
Carry out the monitoring as the written scheme requires and record the results
3.w: The written scheme's monitoring must be carried out and recorded honestly, as it is a legal control measure.

n.1: Recording monitoring as done when it was skipped is falsification.
n.0: Partial monitoring does not meet the requirements of the scheme.
n.2: An operative has no authority to remove monitoring points from the scheme.

3.q: To reduce the risk of scalding while still controlling legionella, what is the correct approach?
o: Lower the hot water storage temperature below 60°C
Keep hot water stored at 60°C or above and fit TMVs where scalding is a risk
Mix a little cold into the storage cylinder
Remove all hot water from vulnerable areas
3.w: Hot water is kept stored hot (at least 60°C) to control legionella, and scalding is managed at the point of use with TMVs.

n.0: Dropping storage below 60°C lets legionella grow; scalding must be controlled another way.
n.3: Removing hot water is impractical and unnecessary when TMVs solve the scalding risk.
n.2: Cooling the stored water below 60°C creates a legionella breeding temperature.

3.q: A tank was sized for a large workforce that has since shrunk, so most of the water is rarely used. What is the risk?
o: The mains pressure will become dangerously high
The tank will run dry every day
The insulation will absorb the extra water
The water stagnates and warms, encouraging bacterial growth
3.w: With low demand the water sits for long periods, warms toward ambient and stagnates, giving bacteria time and conditions to multiply.

n.1: Low demand means the tank is used less, so running dry is unlikely.
n.0: Reduced demand does not raise mains pressure.
n.2: Insulation does not absorb water; it limits heat transfer.

3.q: If a duty holder chooses not to follow the exact advice in ACOP L8, what must they be able to demonstrate?
o: That they saved money by doing less
That another company is now to blame
That the risk no longer needs controlling
That they have controlled the risk to the same standard by another effective method
3.w: Departing from an ACOP is permitted only if you can show you achieved compliance to an equally effective standard.

n.0: Saving money does not justify a lower standard of control.
n.2: The legal duty to control the risk remains regardless.
n.1: Shifting blame does not discharge the duty to control the risk.

3.q: Which of these acts as a nutrient source that helps legionella grow?
o: Fresh air
Clean flowing chlorinated water
Biofilm, scale, rust and organic sediment inside pipes and tanks
Bright sunlight
3.w: Deposits such as biofilm, scale, rust, sludge and organic matter feed the bacteria and shelter them from disinfectant.

n.1: Clean, well-treated flowing water does not provide the nutrients or stagnation the bacteria need.
n.0: Air is not a nutrient source for the bacteria.
n.3: Sunlight is not a food source and does not promote growth inside water systems.

3.q: Which single statement best sums up why showers and spray taps get so much attention in water hygiene?
o: They are the outlets that turn water into a breathable spray, so they must be flushed, cleaned and kept scale-free
They are the cheapest outlets to fit in a building
They are the only outlets fed with hot water
They are the outlets used least often in most buildings
3.w: Showers and spray taps turn water into a breathable spray, which is the main way legionella reaches people, so they must be flushed when little used and cleaned and descaled regularly.

n.1: Cost is not the reason they are a priority for hygiene.
n.2: They are not the only outlets fed with hot water.
n.3: They are not necessarily the least-used outlets; the concern is the aerosol they create.

3.q: Which condition helps legionella to multiply in a water system?
o: Water kept constantly moving and very hot
Water stored below 5°C at all times
Water that is regularly flushed and turned over
Stagnant water with sludge, scale, rust or biofilm to feed on
3.w: Stagnation together with nutrients such as biofilm, scale, rust and sludge provides ideal conditions for legionella to grow.

n.0: Keeping water moving and hot discourages growth.
n.1: Very cold water keeps the bacteria dormant, preventing multiplication.
n.2: Regular flushing removes stagnation and helps prevent growth.

3.q: Why is the blended water leaving a TMV itself a legionella risk?
o: It comes only from the cold supply
It has had all the chlorine removed by the valve
It is warm and sits in the temperature range where legionella can grow
It is stored for long periods before use
3.w: The tepid blended water and the valve internals sit in the bacterial growth range, so TMVs need regular cleaning and servicing.

n.1: A TMV does not strip chlorine from the water.
n.3: The blended water is made on demand, not stored.
n.0: Blended water is a mix of hot and cold, not cold only.

3.q: You find the cold water in a tank reaches 20°C only after standing overnight in a warm plant room. What lasting action helps keep it below 20°C?
o: Add hot water to the tank
Stop recording the tank temperature
Improve insulation and reduce heat gain in the plant room
Paint the tank a darker colour
3.w: Reducing heat gain and insulating the tank helps keep the stored cold water below 20°C.

n.0: Adding hot water would raise the temperature further.
n.1: Stopping recording hides the problem rather than fixing it.
n.3: A darker colour would tend to absorb more heat, not less.

3.q: What is a key aim when designing or running a water system to control legionella?
o: Keep as many unused branches as possible
Store water for as long as possible before use
Keep the water moving and turned over throughout the system
Let water sit still so sediment settles out
3.w: Keeping water moving and turned over stops it stagnating and drifting into the growth range.

n.3: Letting water sit still is exactly what encourages legionella.
n.0: Unused branches become dead legs and should be removed.
n.1: Long storage lowers turnover and raises risk.

3.q: Why might a risk assessment recommend keeping cold water genuinely cold?
o: To reduce the water bill
To keep it below the temperature range where legionella multiplies
To make pipes easier to paint
To make the water taste sweeter
3.w: Keeping cold water below about 20 degrees C helps stop legionella multiplying, which is a core control.

n.3: Temperature control is about safety, not taste.
n.0: It is not primarily a cost-saving measure.
n.2: Painting pipes is unrelated to the temperature control.

3.q: Which everyday feature explains why domestic and workplace showers are treated as a Legionella risk?
o: They deliver a spray of warm water that creates inhalable aerosols
They allow the disease to pass between people using them in turn
They keep water permanently at temperatures that kill all bacteria
They are the only outlets that dispense water for drinking
3.w: Showers spray warm water, generating fine aerosols that can be inhaled; if the water is contaminated with Legionella, this is how infection can occur.

n.3: Showers are not drinking outlets, and drinking is not the route anyway.
n.2: Shower water is often in the warm range that can support growth, not one that kills all bacteria.
n.1: There is no person-to-person spread between successive users.

3.q: Which of these routine tasks would normally be recorded in the monitoring log?
o: Temperature checks, flushing of little-used outlets and TMV servicing
The names of visitors signing in at reception
The daily newspaper headlines
The lunch orders placed by site staff
3.w: Temperature checks, flushing and TMV servicing are control tasks that must be recorded to show the scheme is being followed.

n.1: A visitor book is a separate record, not part of the water monitoring log.
n.3: Lunch orders have nothing to do with water safety monitoring.
n.2: Newspaper headlines are irrelevant to the monitoring record.

3.q: A newly appointed manager finds the site risk assessment was written by an office administrator with no water-hygiene training. What is the concern under L8?
o: The assessment must be rewritten in a different font
The assessment is fine because anyone employed on site may write it
Only assessments written by the water supplier are ever valid
The assessment may not be suitable and sufficient because it was not done by a competent person
3.w: L8 requires the risk assessment to be carried out by a competent person with the necessary knowledge, skills and experience; an untrained author casts doubt on whether it is suitable and sufficient.

n.1: Employment on site does not confer the competence the assessment demands.
n.0: Formatting is irrelevant to the validity of the assessment.
n.2: The water supplier need not write it; a competent person acting for the duty holder may.

3.q: After a thermal disinfection, why is each outlet run for the required time at temperature?
o: To waste hot water on purpose
To warm up the room
To ensure the hot water and heat reach and disinfect every part of the system, including the outlets
To test the water pressure
3.w: Running each outlet at temperature for the set time ensures the heat reaches the full system so no part is missed.

n.0: The controlled run is a necessary part of the method, not deliberate waste.
n.3: The purpose is disinfection by heat, not a pressure test.
n.1: Any room warming is incidental and not the reason for the procedure.

3.q: Which of these does a properly fitting tank lid help to prevent?
o: Water hammer in the pipework
The pump from running dry
Birds, insects and vermin getting into the stored water
Loss of water pressure at the taps
3.w: A close-fitting lid is a physical barrier that stops birds, insects and vermin entering and fouling the stored water.

n.1: Low-water protection for a pump is a separate control, not the lid's job.
n.0: Water hammer is caused by fast-closing valves, not by the tank lid.
n.3: Pressure depends on the tank height, not on whether the lid fits.

3.q: Keeping a calorifier at the correct hot temperature is described in water hygiene guidance as:
o: Something only required in swimming pools
A measure that increases the risk of legionella
A key control measure against legionella
An optional step only needed in summer
3.w: Maintaining correct storage temperature is one of the main control measures for legionella in hot water systems.

n.3: Temperature control is needed year round, not only in summer.
n.0: It applies to hot water systems in all types of building, not only pools.
n.1: Correct hot temperature reduces the risk; it does not increase it.

3.q: What does the term 'sentinel outlets' mean on a hot and cold water system?
o: The outlets located in plant rooms only
The nearest and furthest outlets on a loop or system
Any outlet fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve
The two outlets used most often by staff
3.w: Sentinel outlets are the outlets nearest to and furthest from where water enters the system or loop.

n.3: Frequency of use does not define a sentinel outlet.
n.2: Having a mixing valve does not make an outlet a sentinel.
n.0: Sentinels are chosen by position on the system, not by being in plant rooms.

3.q: When a shower has been dismantled, descaled and disinfected, what is important about how the disinfectant is finally dealt with before hand-back?
o: The head should be refitted still dripping with neat solution
The head and hose should be thoroughly rinsed or flushed through so no harmful residue reaches the user, then refitted
The disinfectant should be poured back into the storage tank
It should be left in the head to keep working indefinitely
3.w: After disinfection the fittings must be rinsed or flushed so that no harmful chemical residue is delivered to the user, then refitted and returned to service; the work and any re-commissioning flush are recorded.

n.3: Leaving disinfectant sitting in the head risks delivering harmful residue to the next user.
n.2: Returning used disinfectant to the storage tank contaminates the stored supply.
n.0: Refitting a head loaded with neat solution would expose the next user to the chemical.

4.q: Which design principle helps reduce legionella risk in pipework?
o: Add extra spare branches for future use
Store as much water as the tank will hold
Make pipes as long and as wide as possible
Keep pipe runs and stored water to the minimum needed
4.w: Minimising pipe length and stored water improves turnover and reduces where stagnant water can sit.

n.2: Long, wide pipes hold more standing water and lower velocity, raising risk.
n.1: Storing excess water reduces turnover and encourages stagnation.
n.0: Spare branches left in place become dead legs.

4.q: SCENARIO: While recording your monthly checks you realise last month's page was never signed or completed. What should you do?
o: Report the gap to the responsible person so it can be investigated and put right
Tear out the incomplete page and throw it away
Do nothing, since only this month's page matters
Fill in last month with invented readings so the log looks complete
4.w: A gap in the records should be reported so it can be investigated and the monitoring regime corrected.

n.3: Inventing readings falsifies safety-critical records and hides whether checks were done.
n.1: Destroying records removes evidence and is never acceptable.
n.2: Ignoring a gap means a lapse in control could go unnoticed.

4.q: 'Stratification' inside a hot water calorifier refers to which of the following?
o: The vessel operating above its rated pressure
A protective scale layer forming on the vessel walls
Layers of water at different temperatures forming, with cooler water settling at the base
Hot water flowing too quickly through the outlets
4.w: Stratification is the layering of water by temperature. Cooler water settles to the bottom while hotter water rises, so the base can sit in the legionella growth range even when the top of the vessel is hot.

n.1: Stratification describes temperature layering of the water, not a scale coating on the walls.
n.0: It is a thermal layering effect, unrelated to the vessel's operating pressure.
n.3: It concerns temperature distribution inside the store, not the flow rate at outlets.

4.q: If the HSE inspects a site and finds the legionella risk is not being managed, which of these can they do?
o: Serve an improvement or prohibition notice and, in serious cases, prosecute
Only offer friendly advice with no powers
Repair the water system themselves for free
Issue a parking ticket
4.w: As the enforcing authority the HSE can serve enforcement notices and bring prosecutions where the law is breached.

n.1: The HSE has real enforcement powers, not just advice.
n.2: The HSE enforces the law; it does not carry out the duty holder's repairs.
n.3: Parking tickets are nothing to do with the HSE's health and safety role.

4.q: Under COSHH, what must be done before employees are exposed to a substance or agent hazardous to health such as legionella?
o: Everyone must be issued a respirator regardless of task
The system must be shut down permanently
A sample must be sent to the police
The risk must be assessed and adequate control measures put in place
4.w: COSHH requires the risk to be assessed and controlled adequately before exposure occurs.

n.0: Respirators are only required where the assessment identifies the need; blanket issue is not the rule.
n.1: Permanent shutdown is not required; the risk is managed, not eliminated by closing systems.
n.2: There is no requirement to involve the police with samples.

4.q: Hot water reaching outlets should achieve at least what temperature within one minute of running?
4.w: HSG274 Part 2 requires hot water to reach the outlet at 50°C or above within one minute of running, confirming hot water is being delivered throughout the system.

n.0: 60°C is the storage standard for the calorifier, not the minimum delivery temperature at outlets.
n.2: 55°C applies to healthcare premises; the general standard at outlets is 50°C.
n.1: 45°C is a mixed-water target after a TMV, not the hot supply temperature at the outlet.

4.q: What is the main purpose of a thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) at an outlet?
o: To blend hot and cold water to a safe temperature and prevent scalding
To kill legionella bacteria inside the pipework
To keep the hot water storage cylinder below 20°C
To boost the water pressure at the tap
4.w: A TMV blends stored hot and cold water down to a safe delivery temperature so users are not scalded at the outlet.

n.2: TMVs control the temperature at the tap, not the storage cylinder, which must stay hot.
n.1: TMVs do not disinfect water; the tepid blended water is actually a legionella risk.
n.3: A TMV is a mixing valve, not a pump, and has no effect on system pressure.

4.q: Which group of outlets is most likely to be prioritised for TMV fitting?
o: Plant-room drain-down points used during maintenance only
Cleaners' sinks and outside taps used only for filling buckets
Kitchen boiling-water taps used for making hot drinks
Baths and showers used by vulnerable people such as the elderly or young children
4.w: TMVs are targeted where a genuine scald risk exists, particularly baths and showers for at-risk users such as the elderly, very young and those unable to react to hot water.

n.1: Cleaners' sinks and external taps generally carry no scald risk to vulnerable users and are not priority TMV locations.
n.2: Boiling-water taps deliver near-boiling water by design and are not fitted with blending TMVs.
n.0: Drain-down points are not user outlets and present no scald risk requiring a TMV.

4.q: At the end of a shift an operative realises they forgot to log a required disinfection check. The honest and correct approach is to:
o: Leave the record blank and hope nobody asks about it
Invent a plausible reading so the record looks complete
Report the missed check to the responsible person so it can be carried out and recorded
Copy the reading from a similar check done last month
4.w: Records must be honest and complete. A missed check is reported so it can be carried out and correctly recorded, rather than invented, copied or hidden.

n.1: Inventing a reading is falsification of a safety record and is never acceptable.
n.0: A blank record with a missed check left unaddressed hides a gap in control.
n.3: Copying an old reading misrepresents the current state of the system and is dishonest.

4.q: Which of these is a reasonable prevention measure the assessment might recommend?
o: Removing redundant pipework and unused outlets that only serve to hold stagnant water
Leaving disused showers connected indefinitely
Adding extra unused tanks in case they are needed later
Fitting more dead-legs to balance the system
4.w: Taking out redundant pipework and outlets removes stagnation points and prevents conditions for legionella growth.

n.2: Extra unused tanks create more storage and stagnation, not less.
n.3: Adding dead-legs increases stagnation risk.
n.1: Leaving disused showers connected keeps a stagnation source.

4.q: A new starter asks whether they should wear a mask around a patient who has Legionnaires' disease to avoid catching it from them. What is the correct response?
o: Only if the patient has a fever, as that is when it becomes contagious
Yes, because the illness spreads easily in enclosed rooms between people
Yes, because coughing spreads Legionnaires' disease directly to others
No, because Legionnaires' disease is not passed from person to person
4.w: Legionnaires' disease is not transmitted person to person; it is caught only by inhaling contaminated aerosols, so no such precaution against the patient is needed.

n.2: Coughing does not transmit the disease between people.
n.1: There is no person-to-person spread in enclosed spaces.
n.0: Fever does not make an infected person contagious; the disease never spreads this way.

4.q: On a hot and cold water system, which outlets are designated the 'sentinel' outlets for routine temperature monitoring?
o: Any two outlets that are used most frequently by occupants
A random sample of one outlet chosen from each floor
Only the outlets fitted with thermostatic mixing valves
The outlets nearest to and furthest from each storage or supply point
4.w: Sentinel outlets are the nearest and furthest outlets on a hot or cold supply, chosen so monitoring captures the extremes of the distribution system.

n.2: TMV-fitted outlets are checked separately; they do not define the sentinel outlets.
n.1: Sentinels are selected by their position on the run, not chosen at random per floor.
n.0: Frequency of use does not determine a sentinel; distance from the source does.

4.q: A colleague suggests signing off a failed disinfection check as a pass to avoid the paperwork of a re-test. This is:
o: Acceptable if the failure was only marginal
Never acceptable, because it hides a real risk and falsifies records
Fine as long as the responsible person is not told
A reasonable time-saving decision on a busy day
4.w: You must never ignore, hide or falsify a failed check. A failure must be recorded honestly and escalated so the cause is corrected, protecting people who use the water.

n.0: A marginal failure is still a failure and must be recorded and acted on, not passed.
n.2: Concealing a failure from the responsible person is exactly what must not happen.
n.3: Falsifying a safety record is never justified by time pressure.

4.q: Cold water in a building should ideally be kept below which temperature to discourage Legionella growth?
4.w: Keeping cold water below 20°C keeps the bacteria dormant and out of the growth range.

n.2: 30°C is well inside the range where Legionella multiplies.
n.3: 40°C is warm enough for rapid growth.
n.1: 45°C is at the top of the active growth range, not a safe cold target.

4.q: What is a 'dead leg' in a water system, and why does it matter?
o: A back-up pump used in emergencies
A pipe that carries only very hot water and is always safe
A length of pipe with little or no flow where water stagnates and bacteria grow
A section of pipe that self-cleans with fresh water
4.w: A dead leg is a low- or no-flow pipe section where stagnant water lets Legionella grow.

n.1: Dead legs are a stagnation problem, not a guaranteed-hot safe zone.
n.0: A dead leg is a pipe section, not a pump.
n.3: A dead leg gets little fresh water, which is exactly why it is a risk.

4.q: Why is an accurate asset register or list of system components valuable to the risk assessment?
o: It ensures all components that could harbour or spread Legionella are accounted for and managed
It is only needed by the finance department for depreciation
It sets the resale value of the plant
It records the guarantee dates for warranty claims
4.w: Knowing every component — tanks, calorifiers, showers, spray taps, cooling plant — lets the assessor account for each potential source and assign controls, so nothing capable of harbouring or spreading the bacteria is overlooked.

n.2: Resale value is a financial matter, not a water-hygiene one.
n.3: Warranty tracking is incidental and not why the register matters here.
n.1: Depreciation accounting is not the assessment's purpose for the register.

4.q: Why should non-approved or unsuitable fittings not be used on a water system?
o: They guarantee the water stays below 20 degrees C
They may leach substances or support growth, contaminating the water
They always cost more than approved fittings
They make the water flow too quickly
4.w: Unsuitable fittings can leach materials into the water or support bacterial growth, so only approved fittings should be used.

n.2: Cost is not the reason; suitability for potable water is.
n.3: Fittings do not generally speed up flow to a dangerous level.
n.0: A fitting does not control water temperature.

4.q: Why are temperature readings recorded and retained rather than simply noted verbally?
o: So the operative can be paid according to the number of outlets tested
Because thermometers legally must upload readings to a central database
To provide an auditable record demonstrating the system is under control over time
Because the water supplier requires a copy before billing the site
4.w: Written records give an auditable trail showing temperatures have been maintained and out-of-range results acted upon, which is central to demonstrating ongoing legionella control.

n.0: Records exist for control and audit, not to calculate an operative's pay.
n.3: Water suppliers do not require temperature logs before billing; the record supports the duty holder's control.
n.1: There is no legal requirement for thermometers to auto-upload to a central database.

4.q: A shower head on a welfare unit is found permanently caked in scale and slime. What does this build-up mainly represent in terms of risk?
o: Scale and biofilm that harbour and feed Legionella and are then aerosolised in use
Evidence the water is too soft and needs hardening
A cosmetic fault only, with no bearing on water safety
Proof the disinfectant dose is set too high
4.w: Scale and biofilm in a head or hose provide a surface and nutrients that shelter and support Legionella; when the shower runs, organisms from that fouling are released in the aerosol.

n.2: It is not merely cosmetic; the deposit is a reservoir for bacterial growth feeding directly into the breathable spray.
n.1: The build-up indicates fouling to be cleaned, not that the water should be made harder.
n.3: Fouling of this kind reflects a lapse in cleaning, not an excessive disinfectant dose.

4.q: When flushing a little-used tap or shower, what tells you it has been flushed for long enough?
o: One minute has passed on the clock
The water stops running
The water looks clear
Hot water runs hot and cold water runs cold
4.w: You flush until the hot runs hot and the cold runs cold, which shows fresh water has drawn through and reached the right temperatures.

n.1: The water should not stop; you keep it running until temperatures are correct.
n.0: A fixed one minute may not be long enough to reach temperature on every outlet.
n.2: Clear-looking water can still be the wrong temperature and stagnant.

4.q: Which two pieces of legislation place general legal duties to control the legionella risk?
o: The Working Time Regulations and the Equality Act
The Road Traffic Act and the Licensing Act
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and COSHH 2002
The Data Protection Act and the Consumer Rights Act
4.w: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the COSHH Regulations 2002 create the legal duties to assess and control the risk.

n.3: These laws cover data and consumer purchases, not water hygiene risk.
n.1: These laws cover driving and alcohol licensing, not legionella control.
n.0: These laws cover working hours and discrimination, not legionella control.

4.q: In broad terms, what does an effective monitoring and records regime allow a duty holder to demonstrate?
o: That every occupant has read the water safety policy
That the building uses less energy than neighbouring premises
That the plumbing was installed by an approved manufacturer
That the control measures identified in the risk assessment are in place and working
4.w: The central value of monitoring records is evidencing that the risk assessment's control measures are being implemented and remain effective over time.

n.1: Energy comparison is unrelated to legionella control evidence.
n.0: Occupant awareness is useful but is not what temperature/flushing records demonstrate.
n.2: Installer approval is a design matter and does not show ongoing control is maintained.

4.q: At a hotel, an elderly guest and a young child both used the same spa pool; the elderly guest developed severe pneumonia and the child was unaffected. What does this most likely reflect?
o: That spa pools cannot actually generate infectious aerosols
That the child must have swallowed the water and so was protected
That the disease was passed from the guest to no one because the child was immune from birth
That the elderly guest, being older, was at greater risk of serious illness
4.w: Older age is a recognised factor increasing the risk of serious Legionella illness, which helps explain why the elderly guest became severely ill while the child did not.

n.0: Spa pools do generate infectious aerosols; that is why one guest fell ill.
n.1: Swallowing water is not protective and is not a route of infection.
n.2: There is no person-to-person spread and no relevant innate immunity; the difference is susceptibility to severe illness.

4.q: A cold water storage cistern is found with a loose-fitting timber board resting on top instead of a proper cover. Under HSG274 Part 2, why is this a significant Legionella risk?
o: It prevents the float valve from operating and starves the outlets of water
It allows light, dust, insects and debris to enter, promoting microbial and Legionella growth
A timber board improves insulation and lowers the stored water temperature below 20°C
It makes the cistern easier to inspect so no further action is needed
4.w: A close-fitting, dust- and insect-proof lid is required to keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin. A loose board lets contaminants and light in, encouraging microbial and Legionella growth.

n.2: Bare timber is not effective insulation and does not seal the cistern; it can also shed contaminants into the water.
n.3: Ease of inspection does not offset the contamination the open gap allows; the cover must still be close-fitting.
n.0: A board on top does not affect float valve operation; the risk is contamination, not supply failure.

4.q: You find water trickling from the overflow pipe continuously. What is the most likely cause?
o: The insect screen is too fine
The tank is too well insulated
The lid is fitting too tightly
The float valve is not shutting off properly
4.w: A continuous overflow usually means the float valve is failing to shut off the inflow at the correct level, so it needs adjusting or replacing.

n.1: Insulation controls temperature and cannot cause a continuous overflow.
n.0: A fine screen restricts insects, not the water level control.
n.2: A tight-fitting lid is desirable and does not cause overflowing.

5.q: A TMV is described as being fitted 'at the point of use'. What does this mean?
o: Right at the tap, shower or bath it serves
On the roof tank
At the boiler room only
At the water meter
5.w: Point of use means the valve is fitted close to the actual outlet, keeping the blended tepid run as short as possible.

n.2: The boiler room is far from the outlet and would leave a long tepid run.
n.3: The water meter is at the incoming supply, not the outlet.
n.1: The roof tank is a storage point, not the point of use.

5.q: Which of the following best explains why simply keeping a system clean of deposits helps control Legionella growth?
o: Removing scale, rust, sludge and biofilm takes away the nutrients and shelter the bacteria rely on
Cleaning permanently lowers the water temperature below 20°C
Cleaning makes the water too pure for aerosols to form
Cleaning replaces the need for any temperature control
5.w: Legionella depends on nutrients and shelter from deposits and biofilm. Removing them by cleaning and descaling reduces the food source and protective habitat, an important part of HSG274 Part 2 control alongside temperature.

n.1: Cleaning removes deposits but does not by itself set the water temperature.
n.3: Cleaning complements temperature control; it does not replace it.
n.2: Water purity does not stop aerosols forming; aerosol is a physical process at outlets.

5.q: Where should a TMV be sited in relation to the outlet it serves?
o: As close to the outlet as practicable
At the incoming cold water main
Halfway along the distribution pipe
As close to the storage cylinder as possible
5.w: Siting the TMV close to the outlet keeps the length of blended tepid water short, limiting where legionella could grow.

n.3: Near the cylinder would leave a long run of tepid blended water in the growth range.
n.1: The cold main is not where blending needs to happen.
n.2: Halfway along still leaves a long section of warm blended water.

5.q: Where a calorifier cannot practically achieve 60°C throughout because of its design, what is the correct course of action?
o: Seek expert advice and apply additional control measures, because temperature alone is now insufficient
Switch the vessel off between uses
Ignore the base temperature and monitor only the flow
Accept a lower storage temperature as normal
5.w: If temperature control cannot be fully achieved, the risk assessment must be reviewed and competent/expert advice sought so that supplementary control measures are put in place; the shortfall is never simply accepted.

n.3: A lower storage temperature must not be accepted as normal; the control gap has to be addressed.
n.1: Switching the vessel off between uses creates stagnation and cooling, increasing risk.
n.2: Ignoring the base leaves the coolest, highest-risk zone unmonitored, which is unsafe.

5.q: Materials used inside a cold water storage tank, such as the lining or float valve, should be:
o: Made of untreated absorbent material
Any spare parts that physically fit
Chosen only for the lowest price
WRAS-approved and suitable for contact with wholesome water
5.w: Components in contact with drinking water must be approved as suitable so they do not taint the water or support bacterial growth.

n.1: Parts that merely fit may not be approved and could contaminate the water.
n.2: Price alone does not ensure a material is safe for contact with drinking water.
n.0: Absorbent, untreated materials can leach substances and harbour bacteria.

5.q: How often should the sentinel outlets (the nearest and furthest on a loop) normally have their temperature checked?
o: Once every five years
Monthly
Twice a day
Only when the building is sold
5.w: Sentinel outlets are checked monthly to confirm the system is holding correct temperatures.

n.0: Once every five years is far too infrequent to spot problems.
n.3: Checking only at sale would leave the system unmonitored for years.
n.2: Twice a day is not the standard routine and is not required.

5.q: A landlord's risk assessment lists 'monthly temperature checks' but names nobody to do them and gives no record sheet. Which required feature of a written scheme is missing?
o: The colour scheme for the plant room walls
The manufacturer's warranty for the boiler
A copy of the tenant's rent agreement
A statement of who is responsible and a means of recording the monitoring
5.w: A written scheme must allocate responsibility for each task and provide for recording the results of monitoring; naming a frequency alone, with no responsible person or record, leaves the scheme incomplete.

n.2: A rent agreement is unrelated to water-hygiene monitoring.
n.0: Decor is not part of the control scheme.
n.1: A boiler warranty does not fulfil the monitoring or responsibility requirement.

5.q: Two calorifiers are installed in parallel with a shared pipework arrangement, but one is kept on standby and rarely used. What is the legionella concern?
o: The standby vessel uses too much energy
Parallel calorifiers cannot be temperature controlled
Water in the idle standby calorifier can stagnate and cool, becoming a reservoir for legionella
The duty calorifier will overheat to compensate
5.w: A rarely used standby vessel can hold stagnant water that cools into the growth range, acting as a reservoir that seeds the system when it is brought into use; standby units should be kept hot or regularly cycled and monitored.

n.0: The concern is stagnation and bacterial growth, not the energy an idle vessel uses.
n.1: Parallel calorifiers can be temperature controlled; the issue is stagnation in the idle unit.
n.3: The duty calorifier does not overheat to compensate; the risk lies in the stagnant standby vessel.

5.q: Why should low-flow or no-flow branches be avoided in system design?
o: Water sits in them and stagnates, encouraging legionella
They use too much disinfectant
They keep the whole system too cold
They carry water too fast to be safe
5.w: Branches with little or no flow hold standing water that stagnates, so good design avoids them.

n.3: The problem is too little flow, not too much.
n.2: Low-flow branches tend to warm up, not keep the system cold.
n.1: Stagnant branches tend to lose disinfectant, not consume the system's supply.

5.q: What is the recorded target for a cold water sentinel outlet?
o: Above 60°C to prevent stagnation
At least 50°C within one minute of running
Between 38°C and 46°C at all times
Below 20°C within two minutes of running
5.w: Cold water should remain below 20°C, measured after running the outlet for up to two minutes, to keep temperatures outside the range that favours legionella growth.

n.1: 50°C in one minute is the hot sentinel target, not the cold requirement.
n.2: 38-46°C describes blended outlet temperatures, which would be dangerously warm for cold water.
n.0: Above 60°C applies to hot water storage, not cold supply.

5.q: An operative is behind on flushing and considers signing the log to show outlets were flushed when they were not. Why must records never be falsified?
o: Because falsified records slow down the next operative's paperwork
Because false records hide real risk, mislead the duty holder and can lead to illness and prosecution
Because the ink used for corrections is expensive to buy
Because the water supplier audits every log entry each week
5.w: Falsifying records conceals uncontrolled risk, prevents proper action, breaches the duty of honesty in ACOP L8 record-keeping, and can contribute to outbreaks and enforcement action.

n.0: The issue is uncontrolled legionella risk and legal duty, not inconvenience to colleagues.
n.3: Water suppliers do not audit internal legionella logs; the duty holder and HSE rely on their accuracy.
n.2: The cost of ink is irrelevant; the point is the safety and legal consequences of dishonesty.

5.q: A sample result is delayed and an operative is tempted to sign off the check as clear before the laboratory reports back. What is correct?
o: Sign it clear now to keep the paperwork moving
Record it as a fail to be safe
Discard the sample and take no result
Wait for the actual result and record what the laboratory reports
5.w: The record must reflect the genuine laboratory result, so the operative waits rather than inventing an outcome.

n.0: Signing off before the result is known falsifies the record.
n.1: Recording an invented fail is also a false entry that misrepresents the test.
n.2: Discarding the sample wastes the test and leaves the question unanswered.

5.q: Which of these is the correct sequence when a routine temperature check finds a reading out of range?
o: Ignore it and move on
Turn hot storage below 60°C to fix it
Record the reading, then report it to the responsible person
Adjust the reading to look acceptable
5.w: An out-of-range reading is recorded honestly and reported to the responsible person for action.

n.0: Ignoring a failure leaves a risk uncontrolled.
n.3: Falsifying records is never acceptable.
n.1: Lowering storage below 60°C increases the Legionella risk.

5.q: A water sample from a shower comes back positive for legionella. What is the appropriate response?
o: Throw the result away and re-sample only if someone falls ill
Do nothing until the next annual review
Report it to the responsible person and follow the plan for disinfection and control
Increase the shower's flow to wash the bacteria away
5.w: A positive result is reported to the responsible person and the agreed remedial and disinfection actions are carried out to bring the system back under control.

n.1: Waiting a year leaves a known contaminated aerosol source in use.
n.0: Discarding a positive result hides a serious risk to health.
n.3: More flow spreads more contaminated aerosol rather than disinfecting the system.

5.q: Which practice would most undermine the control of a shower even if the quarterly cleaning is done on time?
o: Recording the cleaning date accurately in the log
Descaling the head before disinfecting it
Rinsing the head after disinfection
Leaving the shower disconnected but full of stagnant water between quarterly cleans, and never flushing it
5.w: Leaving the shower full of stagnant water and never flushing it between cleans lets Legionella multiply in the retained water regardless of the quarterly service, so regular flushing must accompany periodic cleaning.

n.0: Accurate recording supports control rather than undermining it.
n.1: Descaling before disinfecting is correct practice, as scale would otherwise shield organisms.
n.2: Rinsing after disinfection protects the user from residue and is good practice.

5.q: What does the abbreviation ACOP stand for in relation to L8?
o: Annual Certificate of Practice
Approved Code of Practice
Approved Contractor Order Policy
Advisory Committee on Plumbing
5.w: L8 is the Approved Code of Practice, giving practical advice on complying with the law on legionella.

n.3: There is no such committee behind L8; ACOP is a defined legal term.
n.0: L8 is not a certificate; it is guidance with special legal status.
n.2: ACOP does not refer to a contractor order policy.

5.q: In terms of Legionella, why is a mixer tap or thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) area sometimes described as a higher-risk point for growth?
